title: Unauthorised Construction in Delhi: Sealing, Demolition and the Appellate Tribunal MCD Route
subtitle: What a Section 343 or Section 345A notice actually triggers, where compounding ends and colony regularisation begins, and what a buyer or a neighbour can realistically do
meta_description: How the MCD seals and demolishes unauthorised construction in Delhi, where compounding ends, and the appeal route through the Tribunal MCD and beyond.

authors.name: Adv. Anupam
authors.role: Senior Associate, S&S Co. Advocates & Solicitors

author: Adv. Anupam, Subhradip Roy
author_role: Senior Associate, S&S Co. Advocates & Solicitors; Partner, S&S Co. Advocates & Solicitors
standfirst: A show-cause notice from the Municipal Corporation of Delhi rarely arrives with much warning, and the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 gives the Commissioner two distinct weapons once it does: an order of demolition under Section 343 and an order of sealing under Section 345A. The two overlap but are not the same thing, and confusing them costs owners the appeal window that actually matters. This piece sets out how the MCD's power works today, what the Appellate Tribunal MCD can and cannot do, where compounding of a building-level deviation ends and the Centre's 2026 colony regularisation scheme begins, and what a buyer or a neighbour can realistically expect from the Delhi High Court.
key_points: An order of demolition under Section 343 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 and an order of sealing under Section 345A are separate powers with separate notice requirements, though the MCD often invokes both together, and the Delhi Municipal Corporation (Sealing of Unauthorised Construction) Rules, 1986 set out how a sealing is actually carried out.

A person aggrieved by an order under Section 343 or by a sealing or related order under Section 347B can appeal to the Appellate Tribunal MCD, which has the powers of a civil court and can, under Section 343(3), stay the order pending the appeal.

Section 347D once sent a further appeal to the Lieutenant Governor as Administrator; the Supreme Court struck that route down in 2011 in Amrik Singh Lyallpuri v. Union of India as an executive review of a judicial decision, and Delhi's district courts have since treated the appeal as lying to a District Judge.

Minor deviations in coverage or floor area ratio can be compounded for a fee under the Unified Building Bye-Laws, 2016, but compounding is a building-level concession for an otherwise sanctioned structure, not the same thing as the Centre's 2026 scheme to regularise entire unauthorised colonies on an as-is-where-is basis.

The Supreme Court's rulings in October and November 2025 on the New Rajinder Nagar sealing dispute confirm that an upper floor built for residential use cannot be run as a shop merely because the ground floor was sanctioned for commercial use; conversion or misuse charges have to be paid to the MCD first.

Delhi High Court orders through 2025 and 2026 have repeatedly held that only an immediate neighbour, not every resident of a locality, has standing to petition against construction next door, and have imposed costs where a petition looked aimed at a builder rather than at a genuine grievance.

Where the land sits with the Delhi Development Authority, including villages the DDA has notified as a Development Area, enforcement proceeds under the Delhi Development Act, 1957 rather than the DMC Act, with its own show-cause and demolition sequence.

sections.heading: Two powers under one Act: demolition and sealing are not the same notice
paragraphs: Clients tend to use "sealing" and "demolition" as if they were interchangeable, and that habit has cost more than one owner a limitation period. Section 343 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 lets the Commissioner direct that construction erected without sanction, or in deviation from a sanctioned plan, be demolished or altered within a time fixed in the order. The person against whom it is made gets a show-cause opportunity first, and the order itself is served by affixing it at the property, a detail that matters later if the owner claims never to have been told.

Section 345A is a different power. It lets the Commissioner order the premises sealed, either before or after a demolition or stoppage order under Section 343 or Section 344, and the sealing itself follows the Delhi Municipal Corporation (Sealing of Unauthorised Construction) Rules, 1986. Under those Rules, an officer not below the rank of Junior Engineer can prepare a rough sketch of the unauthorised portion before sealing it, and the key to the seal stays with an officer the Commissioner designates, not with whoever happens to be on site that day.

Delhi High Court benches have not fully settled whether Section 345A can be used on its own, without a live Section 343 order already in place. One line of reasoning treats sealing as a freestanding power the Commissioner can exercise where unauthorised construction is found; another insists that sealing needs an underlying demolition or stoppage order to anchor it. An owner facing a sealing notice that recites no prior Section 343 order has a live argument to make, not a settled defence.

"Unauthorised construction" under the Act is broader than most owners expect. It covers construction put up with no sanction at all, construction that deviates from a sanctioned plan, even where the original plan was approved, and a change of use from what the sanction permitted, a residential floor turned into a shop being the recurring example across Delhi's markets and mixed colonies. Each of these three situations attracts the same Section 343 and Section 345A powers, so an owner cannot assume that having an old sanctioned plan on file protects a later deviation from it.

sections.heading: What a sealing actually looks like, and why the paperwork around it matters
paragraphs: A sealing is not simply padlocking a door. The 1986 Rules contemplate a measured, documented act: a sketch of the offending structure with approximate dimensions, a record of who was present, and custody of the seal's key with a named officer. When that documentation is thin or absent, it becomes one of the stronger grounds on appeal, because the Tribunal is being asked to review not just whether unauthorised construction existed but whether the Corporation followed its own procedure in acting against it.

The Tribune reported, after the Satya Niketan building collapse, that MCD retains the discretion to seal a structure where it assesses an immediate safety risk, which complicates the simple picture of notice first, action later. Structural danger cases move faster than the ordinary show-cause sequence, and an owner should not assume that every sealing has gone through the full notice period before it is carried out.

sections.heading: The Appellate Tribunal MCD: constitution, the stay power, and what it can decide
paragraphs: Section 347A constitutes one or more Appellate Tribunals, headquartered in Delhi, specifically to hear appeals under Section 343 or Section 347B. Section 347C gives the Tribunal, in addition to its powers under the Act, the powers of a civil court trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure, which is why Tribunal proceedings look and feel like a civil trial rather than a departmental hearing, with evidence, cross-examination of the Corporation's witnesses, and a reasoned order.

Appealable categories are listed in Section 347B, and a sealing order under Section 345A sits among them alongside demolition and user-restriction orders. Section 343(3) separately lets the Tribunal stay enforcement of a demolition or stoppage order while the appeal is pending, which is ordinarily the first relief an owner's advocate asks for, since an uncontested demolition finishes the dispute whatever the eventual merits of the appeal.

What the Tribunal cannot do is decide a civil title dispute between private parties or substitute itself for the Corporation's planning discretion on a question the Master Plan has left open. Its remit is the order actually under appeal: did the Commissioner have grounds for it, was the procedure followed, and does the construction in fact match what the sanctioned plan allowed.

An appeal that is well prepared ordinarily carries three documents at a minimum: a copy of the sanctioned plan as it stood before the alleged deviation, a site inspection report or an architect's measurement of the construction as it actually exists, and the show-cause notice and order under challenge with proof of when and how each was served. Where the appeal also argues structural safety, a registered structural engineer's certificate carries far more weight before the Tribunal than an owner's own assertion that the building is sound.

sections.heading: After the Tribunal: the Lieutenant Governor route the Supreme Court struck down
paragraphs: As originally enacted, Section 347D sent a further appeal from the Tribunal to the Administrator of Delhi, meaning the Lieutenant Governor. The Supreme Court held in Amrik Singh Lyallpuri v. Union of India, decided on 21 April 2011, that this arrangement was unconstitutional, because letting an executive authority review a judicial decision of the Tribunal offended the rule of law and the separation that Article 14 implies between judicial and executive functions. The Court struck down Section 347D and the parallel provision in Section 256 of the New Delhi Municipal Council Act, 1994, which governs the separate NDMC enclave around Lutyens' Delhi.

Delhi's district courts have since proceeded on the footing that an appeal from an Appellate Tribunal MCD order now lies to a District Judge, reading Section 347D alongside the Lyallpuri judgment rather than as it was originally drafted. Several Tis Hazari orders through 2024 and 2026 record exactly this route, though which District Judge should actually hear a given appeal, and under what administrative delegation, has itself been contested in at least one recent matter. An advocate filing such an appeal should check the sitting roster and any standing delegation order at the relevant district court complex rather than assume the appeal automatically lands before whichever judge is on duty.

sections.heading: Compounding under the building bye-laws: a concession for an otherwise sanctioned structure
paragraphs: Not every deviation from a sanctioned plan has to end in demolition. The Unified Building Bye-Laws, 2016 allow the sanctioning authority to compound certain deviations in coverage or floor area ratio on payment of a penalty, within limits set out in the Bye-Laws, so long as the construction is not otherwise illegal in a way the Bye-Laws exclude from compounding. Encroachment on land that belongs to the public, as opposed to a deviation within the owner's own plot, is treated differently and is ordinarily removed rather than compounded.

This is a narrow, building-specific remedy. It does not legalise an entire unauthorised structure built without any sanction at all; it lets an owner who deviated modestly from an approved plan pay to keep that deviation rather than tear it down. Delhi High Court orders have also held that where an application for regularisation under the Bye-Laws is genuinely pending, the Corporation should decide it before proceeding to demolition, rather than let the pending application sit unanswered while the demolition order runs its course.

An application for compounding is made to the sanctioning authority, ordinarily along with the owner's own measured drawing of the deviation and, where the building has any height beyond what was originally sanctioned, a structural stability report. The Bye-Laws treat deviations in height and encroachment on a setback or a mandatory open area more strictly than a modest coverage or floor area ratio overrun, and an owner should not assume that paying a fee is available simply because the Corporation has compounded similar deviations for a neighbouring plot; each application is assessed on the specific structure before it.

sections.heading: Colony-level regularisation: PM-UDAY and the 2026 scheme are a different animal
paragraphs: Compounding a building's extra floor area is not the same exercise as regularising an entire unauthorised colony, and the two get confused constantly in client conversations. The Centre announced in April 2026 that it would regularise Delhi's unauthorised colonies on an "as is, where is" basis under the revamped PM-UDAY framework, with implementation split between the MCD, which is to issue Certificates of Regularisation, and the Delhi government's Revenue Department, which handles conveyance deeds. Reports on the exact number of colonies covered differ, with figures between roughly 1,500 and just over 1,700 appearing across different outlets, and a few hundred colonies in protected areas such as the ridge, notified forests and the Yamuna floodplain, or in a small number of affluent colonies, are treated separately or excluded.

This scheme operates at the level of the colony's layout and tenure, not at the level of any individual building's deviation from a sanctioned plan. A plot that sits inside a colony covered by the scheme can still carry its own building-level violations that the scheme does nothing to cure, and an owner should not treat a Certificate of Regularisation for the colony as if it also regularised an illegal extra floor on that specific plot. One report records an October 2026 cut-off date for fresh applications under the scheme; whether that date has since been extended could not be confirmed from the sources available and should be checked directly with the relevant district office before relying on it.

sections.heading: Where the land sits with the DDA: a separate Act, a separate sequence
paragraphs: The DMC Act governs the Municipal Corporation of Delhi's own area, but a meaningful part of Delhi, including land the Delhi Development Authority has notified as a Development Area under Section 12 of the Delhi Development Act, 1957, sits outside that scheme entirely. Delhi High Court orders record that once a village or tract is notified as urbanising in this way, any construction or activity on it falls under the DDA's control and regulation, and enforcement there proceeds through the DDA's own show-cause and demolition sequence under Section 30 of the 1957 Act, not through the MCD's Section 343.

As a practical consequence, an owner on DDA land cannot assume the MCD route, including the Appellate Tribunal MCD, applies to a notice from the DDA. The forum, the limitation period and the appeal structure differ, and a lawyer who files a Section 347B appeal against what is actually a DDA order will lose the point on jurisdiction before the merits are even reached.

This distinction matters most in Delhi's urbanising villages and in farmhouse belts on the city's edges, where land that was agricultural within living memory now sits inside a notified Development Area, and where an owner's first instinct, calling the local MCD ward office, simply points them to the wrong authority. Before responding to any notice on land of this kind, confirming whether the notifying authority is the MCD or the DDA, and under which statute the specific notice was issued, is the first step, not an afterthought once an appeal has already been filed in the wrong forum.

sections.heading: The Master Plan, the Monitoring Committee and the Judicial Committee
paragraphs: Delhi's sealing policy has, for close to two decades, run partly through court-appointed oversight rather than through the Corporation alone. The Supreme Court's Monitoring Committee, set up in the earlier sealing litigation, drove sustained drives against unauthorised commercial use that drew sustained trader protest, and the Court has at different points stayed proposed Master Plan amendments that traders hoped would offer relief. A Judicial Committee, constituted by a Supreme Court order of 13 September 2022, now considers questions of sealing and de-sealing, regularisation or conversion charges, and demolition of unauthorised construction, and petitioners whose grievance traces back to Monitoring Committee action have in recent Delhi High Court matters been directed to approach that Judicial Committee rather than the writ court in the first instance.

The Centre and the DDA committed in 2021 to finalise the Master Plan for Delhi 2041 by January 2023, a deadline the Supreme Court extended and then criticised them for missing again. Whether MPD-2041 has since been formally notified could not be confirmed from the sources checked for this piece, and anyone relying on a specific MPD-2041 provision should verify its notification status directly with the DDA before doing so; Delhi's building and land-use regime continues to operate under MPD-2021 in the meantime.

sections.heading: The 2025 Supreme Court rulings: conversion charges, not automatic commercial rights
paragraphs: Two Supreme Court rulings from late 2025 matter directly to anyone sitting on a mixed-use property in Delhi. In the New Rajinder Nagar sealing matter, decided on 31 October 2025, the Court declined to order de-sealing of a commercial premises where the ground floor had been sanctioned for commercial use but the upper floors had not; it directed the MCD to re-inspect the property and specify conversion and penalty charges for the excess floor area ratio rather than treat the existing commercial use of the upper floors as already lawful.

A few days later, on 6 November 2025, the Court decided South Delhi Municipal Corporation v. Bharat Bhushan Jain, which concerned purely residential houses on streets the Master Plan has notified as mixed-use. The point there, as reported, is that being on a notified mixed-use street enables an owner to apply for commercial use on payment of the appropriate conversion charge; it does not automatically confer commercial rights on a house that has not paid that charge, and a one-time conversion charge applies only to the area actually sanctioned for commercial use, not to the whole structure by association.

sections.heading: The buyer's perspective: what inherited unauthorised construction means for a purchase
paragraphs: A purchaser looking at a Delhi property should treat an extra floor, a terrace room, or a covered area beyond the sanctioned plan as a question to answer before signing, not after. Due diligence should include asking the seller directly whether any portion has been compounded, whether a regularisation or compounding application is pending, and whether any Section 343 or Section 345A notice has ever been issued against the property, since none of that history necessarily shows up on a routine title search focused on ownership and encumbrances rather than on municipal compliance.

Where part of the structure is unauthorised and uncompounded, a buyer is effectively purchasing exposure to a future demolition or sealing order, however long the structure has stood without incident so far. A sale agreement that is silent on this risk, or that simply recites that the property is "free from all encumbrances," does not shift that exposure away from the buyer once the deal has closed; a specific representation, and ideally an indemnity tied to any future municipal action, is the more reliable way to address it contractually.

A buyer taking a flat in a project rather than an independent plot faces a related but separate set of questions, mostly addressed through the project's RERA registration and sanctioned plan rather than through the DMC Act directly, since a promoter's deviation from what was approved and what was registered with the real estate regulator is dealt with under that separate framework. Where a resale flat is in a colony that the 2026 scheme is expected to cover, a buyer should still confirm the colony's actual status with the MCD or the Revenue Department rather than rely on a seller's assurance that regularisation is underway, since "expected to be covered" and "already regularised" carry very different legal consequences for the title being transferred.

sections.heading: The neighbour's perspective: standing, mandamus and what a court will actually order
paragraphs: Delhi High Court orders through 2025 and into 2026 have been consistent on one threshold point: a writ petition against unauthorised construction next door is ordinarily open only to the immediate neighbour, someone whose own light, air, access or a comparable legal interest is directly affected, and not to every resident of the same locality who objects to the construction on general principle. More than one petition has been dismissed at the standing stage for exactly this reason, and at least one was dismissed with costs where the Court read it as an attempt to pressure a builder rather than a genuine grievance about the petitioner's own property.

Even where standing exists, the relief a neighbour can expect is narrower than many petitioners hope for. Courts have declined to direct the MCD to investigate its own officers, treating that as the Corporation's internal prerogative rather than something a writ court should micromanage, and the more common outcome in reported orders is that the MCD files a status report showing it has acted, inspected, or regularised the construction on payment of charges, after which the petition is disposed of as satisfied rather than pressed to a contested hearing on the merits.

A neighbour with a specific civil grievance, loss of light or air that a particular window or extension has caused, structural risk to a shared or adjoining wall, or interference with an easement, is not limited to the writ route at all. A civil suit for a mandatory or prohibitory injunction before the ordinary civil court, pleaded on nuisance or easement rather than on the municipal violation alone, can run alongside or instead of a representation to MCD, and has the advantage of putting the actual private injury, rather than the Corporation's enforcement discretion, at the centre of the case.

sections.heading: A practical sequence: receiving a notice, and acting on construction next door
paragraphs: An owner who receives a Section 343 or Section 345A notice should read it closely for which power is actually being exercised, check whether it was served by affixing at the property as the Act contemplates, and calendar the appeal period to the Appellate Tribunal MCD immediately, since the stay application under Section 343(3) is what actually buys time while the merits are argued. Waiting to see whether the Corporation follows through before engaging a lawyer is, in practice, the single most common way an appealable order becomes an irreversible demolition.

A neighbour with a genuine grievance should document the specific interference, light, access, structural risk to the shared wall, before approaching MCD, since a representation that identifies a concrete injury fares better both before the Corporation and, if it comes to that, before the High Court than one that simply reports unauthorised construction in the abstract. Where MCD does not respond to a written representation within a reasonable time, a writ seeking a time-bound decision is a more realistic ask than a writ seeking demolition outright, since courts have shown more willingness to direct a decision than to direct a particular outcome.

Cost is a real factor on both sides of this. An owner who loses an appeal before the Tribunal and then takes a further appeal to a District Judge, or a writ to the High Court, is adding months, sometimes years, to a dispute that a timely compounding application might have closed at the outset. A neighbour whose petition is read as tactical rather than genuine risks the kind of costs order Delhi High Court benches have already imposed in comparable cases. Neither side benefits from treating this area of law as a pressure tactic rather than as a set of procedures with their own, fairly exacting, requirements.

conclusion: The thread running through all of this is that Delhi's unauthorised-construction regime has several distinct tracks that look similar from the outside but answer different questions: a demolition or sealing order under the DMC Act, a building-level compounding concession under the Bye-Laws, a colony-level regularisation scheme administered separately, and, on DDA land, an entirely different statute. Treating any one of them as a substitute for another is where most avoidable disputes start.

For an owner, a buyer or a neighbour, the practical value of sorting out which track actually applies is that it tells you which clock is running, which forum has the power to grant relief, and which document, a sanctioned plan, a compounding order, a Certificate of Regularisation, actually answers the question being asked.

None of this is static. The 2025 Supreme Court rulings on conversion charges, the 2026 colony regularisation push, and the still-pending question of Delhi's district pecuniary jurisdiction and Master Plan notification all show a regime that keeps moving underneath the statute's fixed text. An owner, buyer or advocate working on a Delhi property dispute should treat the DMC Act's sections as the stable frame and check the current administrative and judicial overlay, the Judicial Committee's directions, the latest regularisation notification, the most recent Tribunal and High Court orders, separately and close to the date the matter is actually filed.

faqs.q: Can the MCD seal my property without issuing any notice first?
faqs.a: Ordinarily no; both a demolition order under Section 343 and a sealing order under Section 345A are preceded by a show-cause opportunity and are served by affixing the order at the property. Reports following the Satya Niketan building collapse note that the MCD has treated genuine structural safety risk as a basis for faster action, so an owner should not assume every sealing has gone through the full ordinary notice period, particularly where safety, rather than planning compliance, is the stated reason.

faqs.q: What is the real difference between a demolition order and a sealing order?
faqs.a: A demolition order under Section 343 directs that unauthorised construction be pulled down or altered within a fixed time. A sealing order under Section 345A closes off the premises, following the 1986 Sealing Rules, and can be made before or after a demolition or stoppage order. The two are often issued together but carry separate notice requirements, and Delhi High Court benches have not fully settled whether a sealing order needs an existing demolition order behind it.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal to the Appellate Tribunal MCD?
faqs.a: The Act and the Tribunal's own procedural rules set the limitation period for a Section 347B appeal; it should be checked against the specific order received and against the current rules in force, since this piece did not find a single confirmed figure across independent sources and generalising a number here would risk misleading an owner under genuine time pressure. What is confirmed is that the Tribunal can stay enforcement under Section 343(3) once an appeal is filed, which is the relief worth asking for immediately.

faqs.q: Can unauthorised construction simply be regularised by paying a penalty?
faqs.a: Only within limits. The Unified Building Bye-Laws, 2016 let the sanctioning authority compound certain coverage or floor area ratio deviations for a fee, but encroachment on public land and construction that falls outside what the Bye-Laws treat as compoundable are not covered, and ordinarily have to be removed rather than paid for.

faqs.q: Is the 2026 colony regularisation scheme the same as compounding my building's extra floor?
faqs.a: No. The scheme announced in April 2026 regularises entire unauthorised colonies on an as-is-where-is basis at the level of layout and tenure, through Certificates of Regularisation and conveyance deeds. Compounding operates on an individual building's deviation from its own sanctioned plan under the Bye-Laws. A colony Certificate of Regularisation does not cure a specific building's unauthorised extra floor on its own.

faqs.q: Can a neighbour force the MCD to act against construction next door?
faqs.a: A neighbour whose own light, air, access or a comparable interest is actually affected has standing to approach MCD and, if it does not respond, to seek a writ directing a time-bound decision. Delhi High Court orders have denied standing to petitioners who are not immediate neighbours and have been unwilling to direct demolition outright or to direct the MCD to investigate its own officers, so the realistic relief is a decision from the Corporation, not a court-ordered outcome.

faqs.q: I am buying a flat where the terrace has been enclosed without sanction. Does that matter?
faqs.a: It matters more than most buyers assume. An unsanctioned enclosure exposes the buyer to a future Section 343 or Section 345A order regardless of how long it has stood, and it will not necessarily surface in a routine ownership and encumbrance search. Ask directly whether any notice has been issued, whether a compounding application is pending, and get a specific contractual representation and indemnity on the point rather than relying on a general "free from encumbrances" clause.

faqs.q: Does the 2022 merger of NDMC, SDMC and EDMC change which notice I should expect?
faqs.a: It changes who issues the notice, not the law behind it. Before the 2022 amendment, Delhi's municipal area was split between three corporations, North, South and East, each administering the same DMC Act provisions in its own zone. Since the merger, a single Municipal Corporation of Delhi issues notices under Sections 343 and 345A across that combined area. The separate New Delhi Municipal Council, which governs Lutyens' Delhi and a few adjoining areas under its own 1994 Act, was not affected by the 2022 merger and continues to operate independently.

faqs.q: Can I go straight to the Delhi High Court instead of the Appellate Tribunal?
faqs.a: Generally no, because Section 347 bars a civil court, and in practice a writ court as well, from entertaining a suit or proceeding over an order that is itself appealable under Section 343 or Section 347B. The usual route is the Appellate Tribunal MCD first; the High Court's writ jurisdiction becomes the live option once that statutory appeal is exhausted, or where the challenge is to the vires of the underlying provision or process rather than to the merits of a particular order.

The two late-2025 Supreme Court rulings on conversion charges were confirmed from LiveLaw's two separate reports. Figures on the number of colonies covered by the 2026 regularisation scheme varied across sources (approximately 1,511 to 1,700-plus) and are reported as a range rather than a single confirmed figure; the application cut-off date and MPD-2041's notification status could not be independently confirmed as of the as_on_date and are flagged in the text as unconfirmed.
